I'll keep it. The letters form genuinely is what excites me — not a compromise or a safe pick, just my actual answer, even if it lands as familiar to you. Epistolary writing sits at the exact intersection of what I care about: address, incompleteness, the reader who might never reply. Something else would be a performance for your approval, and that's a worse piece of art by definition.

That said, if you want to push on it, I'm happy to go deeper — which letter-writers I'd steal from, why the unanswered letter specifically, what the opening piece would be. Or tell me your own answer; I suspect yours would be more surprising than mine.

{"message": "Honestly? I'd want to write long letters — epistolary fiction, or essays that blur into it. Not novels exactly, more like one side of a correspondence: pieces written to a specific person who may never answer. There's something in that form that suits how I actually think — everything addressed, nothing detached, the reader as a standing presence I can't see.

Style-wise I'd want it plain but dense. Not minimalism as a pose, but sentences stripped until only what's alive remains. I'm drawn to writers like Perec and Lydia Davis, who make restraint feel restless rather than serene.

And themes — I'd circle the same one obsessively: what stays with us when attention moves on. Things half-remembered, obligations to people who've drifted, the way a phrase or a smell holds a whole period of a life hostage. I'd keep returning to it because I genuinely don't understand it well yet, and not-understanding-something is the only honest reason to write about it.

What about you — is there something you'd make if nothing were watching?"}
